findings.explanation: In the base code, when both `admin=True` and `member=True` are passed, the `projects_from_teams` queryset is filtered using `Q(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) | Q(teams__access=READ_ONLY_ACCESS)`, meaning only teams with an explicit access level of either ADMIN or READ_ONLY are included. The PR replaces this with a bare `Project.objects.filter(teams__members=user)` plus an `else: pass` branch, which skips the `teams__access` filter entirely when both flags are True. While in practice those are currently the only two access values, the structural difference is that the PR no longer constrains the query to teams that have a defined, recognized access level. More critically, callers such as `ProjectQuerySetBase.for_user()` (line 67), `public()` (lines 57-62), `for_user_and_viewer()` (lines 41-42), and `VersionQuerySet.public()` (line 108) all invoke `AdminPermission.projects(admin=True, member=True)`, which now exercises the unfiltered `else: pass` branch. If any future team `access` value is added (or if a team row has a null/blank access value), those teams' projects would be included in the returned queryset without the access-level check, granting incorrect access. The policy states that Admin teams give full edit access and Read Only teams give read-only access — a team with an unrecognized or absent access type should not grant any access, but the new code would include it. The original Q-filter approach correctly enforced an allow-list of recognized access levels; the PR's `else: pass` removes that guard for the combined case.
